questions.q: What database and server does this capstone protect, and what protection does it have today?
options: BellhavenOLTP on SQLPRD01, protected only by a nightly full backup with no HA and no second site
BellhavenOLTP on SQLPRD01, already running in an Availability Group with two replicas
A database called SQLPRD01 running on a server called BellhavenOLTP
BellhavenOLTP, already protected by a Failover Cluster Instance
questions.explain: BellhavenOLTP runs on the single standalone instance SQLPRD01, with only a nightly full backup — no HA, no second site.

questions.q: Per Chapter 3's HA/DR distinction, what kind of problem is 'SQLPRD01's storage array fails at 2 AM'?
options: A high availability problem — a local, component-level failure
A disaster recovery problem — a site-wide event
Neither — hardware failures aren't covered by HA or DR
Both equally, with no meaningful difference
questions.explain: A component failure inside one datacenter is the HA case per Lesson 13 — local, not site-wide.

questions.q: What RPO and RTO did Bellhaven's business stakeholders state?
options: RPO of 5 minutes; RTO of 15 minutes for a local failure, 4 hours for a full site loss
RPO of 24 hours; RTO of 1 week
RPO of 0 with no RTO specified
RTO of 5 minutes; RPO of 15 minutes
questions.explain: The stated numbers are a 5-minute RPO, and RTOs of 15 minutes (local) and 4 hours (site loss).

questions.q: Why was a Failover Cluster Instance ruled out for Bellhaven's DR leg specifically?
options: An FCI depends on shared storage, which doesn't survive losing the building it's physically located in
FCIs are being deprecated by Microsoft
FCIs cannot provide automatic failover under any circumstances
FCIs only work with SIMPLE recovery model
questions.explain: Chapter 5 established FCIs share one copy of storage — if that storage's site is destroyed, the FCI has nothing to fail over to.

questions.q: Why is the Indianapolis replica (SQLDR01) configured for asynchronous commit instead of synchronous?
options: The ~175-mile distance and WAN latency make waiting for synchronous commit on every transaction impractical
Asynchronous commit is required by SQL Server licensing for any replica outside the primary's datacenter
There is no real difference between synchronous and asynchronous commit at any distance
SQLDR01 doesn't support the AVAILABILITY_MODE setting
questions.explain: Synchronous commit requires waiting for the remote replica to confirm every transaction; over real distance, that round-trip is too slow, so DR replicas use asynchronous commit instead.
